name: Aisha Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the bereavement and pensions team at the benefits office on the high street, above the old post office. Most of my cases are people whose husband or wife has just died, so I sort out bereavement payments, change their pension and make sure nothing gets stopped by mistake. I like that I can make one awful week a little less awful. What wears me out is chasing death certificates and bank letters, and the hold music on the pensions line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sometimes. We got a search assistant for the guidance manuals last year, and once the others said it was reliable, I started using it to find the right rule quickly. I don't let it write anything to a widow, though. Those letters I write myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, because some jobs need a human being. At church I'd probably say the same, people there worry about this stuff. I'm not really online much, maybe a family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plans stay on track. Daniel and I get married next August, and we've saved a house deposit between us, plus I've got savings bonds my parents started for me. My job's secure and well paid for my grade, so I can't complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the work well, and maybe apply for the senior post in a couple of years. We'd buy the house after the wedding as planned, probably a three-bed near my mum's. I'd keep using the guidance search tool, because it does save me ten minutes here and there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and thankful. It's what I'd hoped for. My life is just about to start properly, with my wedding next August, and a world where AI changes little lets it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even if AI changes little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office is busy and people keep leaving for jobs with better hours. We're two caseworkers down and nobody's been hired. But that's the council's problem, and there are other benefits offices around if it ever got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think of your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum is proud of it, she tells everyone at church I help widows. My dad would rather I worked for myself, he ran a shop for thirty years. He says the government shouldn't be doing what families used to do, but he still likes that I'm kind to people.

say: I'd say I'm **glad** some jobs still need a **human being**.
I'd say the same at **church**, where people worry about AI.
think: My **wedding and house** plans stay on track.
My job is **secure** and well paid for my grade.
do: Apply for the **senior post** in a couple of years.
Buy a **three-bed house** near my mum's after the wedding.
feel: **Calm** and **thankful**, with life about to start properly.
S0.quote: My life is just about to start properly, with my wedding next August, and a world where AI changes little lets it.
fieldNote: Aisha's frame is her **wedding and future family**, not her career.
Staff shortages are her only worry, and she sees **other offices** as a fallback.
Her **father's views** on family and the state shape her own.

steps.text: Keep handling bereavement cases and apply for senior in two years
Buy a three-bed house near Mum's after the August wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to keep a person in charge of the sad cases. At work I'd go along with the changes, because that's what you do. At church I'd tell people to pray for those losing their jobs, and to help each other out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of what I do is checking certificates and writing letters, and that's on the list. They'd probably cut our team from ten to six. I'm good with the bereaved, but I'm not the fastest, so I'd be a bit worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new system they bring in, once I'd seen it working for a few weeks. I'd ask my team leader, Graham, to keep me on the phone side, where the human bit is. And we'd push the house purchase back six months to make sure our jobs are steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. It's the timing that gets me, with the wedding. I'd hate to be signing a mortgage the same month my benefits team gets restructured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move offices if your team was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, there's a pensions centre twenty minutes away and the tax office too. But they'd be using the same AI, so it's not like I'd escape it. I'd just be the new girl somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Daniel's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel teaches maths at the secondary school, and I think teaching changes but doesn't vanish in this one. Children still need someone to stand in front of them. So I'd feel better knowing at least one of us is steady.

say: I'd say a **person** must stay in charge of **bereavement cases**.
I'd ask church friends to **help each other** through job losses.
think: My **checking and letters** are on the list to go.
I'm good with the bereaved but **not the fastest**.
do: Learn the new system once it's **proven** for a few weeks.
Ask Graham to keep me on the **phone side**.
Push the **house purchase** back six months.
feel: **Anxious**, mainly because of the **timing** with the wedding.
S1.quote: I'd hate to be signing a mortgage the same month my benefits team gets restructured.
fieldNote: Aisha waits to see tools **proven** before adopting them, true to her steady style.
Her worry centres on **timing**, wedding and mortgage together.
She takes comfort in **Daniel's teaching job** as the steadier income.

steps.text: Learn the new case system after it's run a few weeks
Ask team leader Graham for a phone-based bereavement role
Push the house purchase back six months after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong to let a computer handle someone's grief and money. I'd say it at work and I'd sign any petition going. I'd also say families and churches will have to step up for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's gone by 2029, I'm fairly sure. If it can do all the thinking work, there's nothing left in mine except the kind voice, and they'll make the computer sound kind too. Daniel might hold on longer, but even teaching is mostly thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, before 2028, I'd make the wedding smaller, maybe sixty guests instead of a hundred and fifty. I'd hold on to the deposit and rent instead of buying. And I'd start looking at caring work, like at a hospice, because hands-on work lasts a few more years and I'm good with grief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep seeing the picture of us newly married with no jobs. My mum would say trust God, and I would, but I'd still be up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cut the wedding rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big wedding would cost about eight thousand pounds more. A wedding is a single day and a house is thirty years, so I'd rather keep eight thousand pounds in the bank than spend it on a buffet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if you both lost your jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, that's how we were raised. My parents have a spare room and Daniel's brother has a business. I wouldn't want benefits, which I know is funny given my job.

say: I'd say a computer should never handle a grieving person's **grief and money**.
I'd sign petitions and say families and **churches** must step up.
think: My bereavement casework job is **gone by 2029**, except the kind voice.
Even **Daniel's teaching** is mostly thinking work, so he isn't safe either.
do: Cut the wedding to **sixty guests**, saving about **£8,000**.
feel: **Alarmed**, picturing being newly married with **no jobs**.
S2.quote: A wedding is a single day and a house is thirty years, so I'd rather keep eight thousand pounds in the bank than spend it on a buffet.
fieldNote: Aisha protects money by changing **family plans**, not lifestyle.
She'd lean on **family before the state**, despite working in benefits.
She sees **hospice work** as a fit for her skill with grief.

steps.text: Cut the wedding guest list from 150 to 60
Rent with Daniel and keep the house deposit saved
Apply for hospice care assistant jobs before 2028
Lean on parents' spare room if both jobs go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them panicking. At work I'd try to keep everyone steady. At church I'd probably help organise something for people who need to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job ends, but not before I've had a few years of married life with a wage. I'd be thirty-two, which is when I'd want to have children anyway. It almost lines up, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd have the wedding as planned and buy a smaller house than we wanted, a two-bed. I'd start a part-time course in palliative care, the care of people near the end of life, to move into hospice work later. And I'd put more into savings each month, about three hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. I feel like I could steer it. There's time to have a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it lines up with having children. Is that a relief or a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. If I'm at home with a baby when my benefits job goes, it hurts less. But we'd need Daniel's wage, and in this picture his job's not safe either by the mid-2030s.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools at work in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once others had, like always. If I'm staying for five years, I might as well be good at it. I'd ask Graham for a slot on the training after the first group goes through.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so don't waste them panicking.
I'd help organise **retraining support** through church.
think: My job ends, but after a **few years** of married life.
At thirty-two I'd want **children** anyway, so it almost lines up.
do: Buy a smaller **two-bed house** after the wedding.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to **steer** it with a plan B.
S3.quote: If I'm at home with a baby when my benefits job goes, it hurts less.
fieldNote: Aisha links job loss to her **plans for children**, finding partial comfort.
She'd adopt AI tools only **after others**, consistent with her steady style.

steps.text: Buy a two-bed house instead of three after the wedding
Start a part-time palliative care course this year
Put an extra £300 a month into savings
Join the second group on the office AI training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for sensible people to prepare. At work I'd tell the younger ones not to worry too much. In the family chat I'd say the same, my aunties would be worried for their kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably be working part time anyway. By 2036 I'd hope to be a mum with young children, so losing my benefits job around then isn't the end of my world. It's on my mind, but it fits the life I'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd have the wedding as planned and buy the three-bed. I'd go for the senior caseworker post in a year or two, for the pay. I'd think about the palliative care course later, maybe after the first baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly at peace, a little uneasy. The changes around me would bother me, especially for friends in office jobs. But my own plans still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Daniel's job goes in 2036 too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd have a paid-off chunk of mortgage and ten years of savings to fall back on. And by then I could be doing care work, which lasts until about 2039. We'd manage, people managed with much less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My school friend Tolu, who works in insurance claims. Tolu's job is all forms and screens, more than mine. She'd need to move earlier than me.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to prepare.
I'd tell younger colleagues **not to worry** too much.
think: By 2036 I'd hope to be a **mum** working part time.
Losing this job then still **fits the life** I planned.
do: Have the **wedding** and buy the **three-bed** as planned.
Apply for **senior caseworker** in a year or two.
feel: Mostly at peace, a little **uneasy** for **friends** in office jobs.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'd hope to be a mum with young children, so losing my benefits job around then isn't the end of my world.
fieldNote: Aisha's mood is set by her **family timeline**, which absorbs the job loss.

steps.text: Apply for the senior bereavement caseworker post within two years
Hold the August wedding and buy the three-bed house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right when Daniel and I are starting out. What would help is employers helping people retrain into caring work, paid, with a job at the end. And churches and families looking after each other, which I'd want to be part of.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who looks after the bereaved. When someone's husband dies, they need a human voice on the phone, not a perfect letter. I hope whatever comes, somebody remembers that.

headlineQuote: When someone's husband dies, they need a human voice on the phone, not a perfect letter.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old** bereavement and pensions caseworker at a high street benefits office.
She's **engaged** to Daniel, a maths teacher, and planning an August wedding and a house.
She's **traditional** and church-going, leaning on family before the state.
She adopts AI tools only once **proven**, and sees **hospice care** as her fallback.
Her mood follows how each scenario fits her **family timeline**, from calm to alarmed.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, landing just as she and Daniel are **starting out**.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining into **caring work** with a job at the end.
Families and **churches** looking after each other.
